analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on consumer loans and credit cards at 15% nationwide.
analysis.headline: A bill to cap consumer interest rates at 15% attracted 10 House sponsors but never got a committee vote, dying quietly after 19 months.
analysis.plain_summary: The Loan Shark Prevention Act would have capped the annual percentage rate on any consumer loan or credit card at 15%, including all fees, with lenders that overcharge owing back every dollar of interest they collected. It would have preserved stricter state rate caps and let the Federal Reserve temporarily lift the ceiling for up to 18 months if market rates rose and lenders' finances were threatened. Credit unions were exempt from the cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Households carrying high-interest credit card balances, payday loans, and other consumer debt would pay sharply less in interest, and borrowers who were overcharged could sue to recover everything they paid. People in states with no rate cap would gain the most, since the 15% federal ceiling would apply where state law does not go lower.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households carrying high-interest credit card and loan debt

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any extension of consumer credit at 15% — or the lower cap in the borrower's state — counting all finance charges, and blocks lenders from dodging the cap with extra fees (total fees cannot exceed finance charges).

Gives borrowers a way to fight back: a lender that knowingly charges above the cap forfeits all the interest on the loan, and a borrower can sue within two years to recover the entire amount of interest and fees paid.
Does not override stronger state consumer protections — state laws capping rates lower than 15% still apply.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, banks, payday lenders, and other consumer lenders would lose interest revenue, since typical credit card rates run well above 15%. Some lenders would respond by offering less credit to borrowers with poor credit histories, so the riskiest borrowers could find legal credit harder to get.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers, banks, and payday lenders

drawbacks.text: A hard 15% cap would likely push lenders to stop serving the riskiest borrowers, since lenders price credit to risk; people with low credit scores could lose access to legal credit and be left with worse options — the standard tradeoff of any strict rate cap.

The cap is not absolute: the Federal Reserve could raise it for up to 18 months at a time if market interest rates rose and lenders' safety and soundness were threatened, weakening the protection when it might matter most.
Credit unions are fully exempt from the cap, letting them keep charging above 15% while banks and other lenders cannot — a carve-out that blunts the cap's reach for some borrowers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households paying rates well above 15% on credit cards and small loans, the cap would have delivered real, direct savings, and the private right to claw back overcharged interest gave it teeth that many consumer laws lack. The honest cost is access: a strict cap priced for the average borrower inevitably means some high-risk borrowers lose legal credit options, and the bill — never debated in committee — was never analyzed or modified to address that. The credit union exemption and the Fed's escape valve also trimmed what the cap would have covered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, joined by eight original cosponsors, for a total of 10 House sponsors — all Democrats.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, which is where it stayed; the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no further action of any kind.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still sitting in committee and the 15% cap never coming to a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers, banks, and payday lenders came out ahead: they kept charging rates above 15% with no federal cap and no refund liability, while borrowers with high-rate debt got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and high-interest lenders

for.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, which would cap consumer interest rates at 15%.

for.name: 9 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Thompson of Mississippi, Pressley, Tlaib, Omar, Clay, Jackson Lee, Velazquez, and others).

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Maxine Waters)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over consumer credit
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the record shows no action after the initial referral in May 2019.

against.name: Banking and small-dollar lending industry groups
against.role: Lenders whose revenue depends on interest rates above 15%
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed federal interest rate caps as a matter of industry position; no record of action on this specific bill appears in the sources.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats — 9 of 231 House Democrats cosponsored — and no Republican signed on or brought the bill forward; the bill never reached a roll-call vote, so no formal party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: A 15% APR cap would end the business model outright, since these lenders charge effective annual rates in the triple digits. Borrowers using them would either pay far less or lose this credit option entirely.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and major banks
industries.note: Standard card APRs typically run above 15%, so the cap would cut a major revenue stream — and the bill's refund provision would let borrowers recover interest already collected over the prior two years. The industry's interest in blocking the cap runs against borrowers who carry balances.

The bill explicitly exempts insured credit unions from the cap, giving them a pricing advantage over capped banks and card issuers. But because they are exempt, their own members' rates stay uncapped too.
